study.research_problem: Vertebral-body replacement implants can mismatch endplates, concentrate stress, subside into cancellous bone, and fail mechanically. Strut-based porous artificial vertebral implants may trade lower stiffness for weak junctions and local stress concentration, motivating a Gyroid TPMS architecture.
study.exact_gap: TPMS Gyroid porous artificial vertebral implants had not been evaluated with a high-resolution porous finite-element model and matched mechanical tests for vertebral-interface stress, implant stress, static compression, and subsidence. The study does not test in-vivo fusion or clinical outcomes.
study.objective_or_hypothesis: Design a 60% nominal-porosity Gyroid AVI with the same external contour as a traditional strut/'diamond-like' porous AVI, and test whether it lowers modeled peak stress, increases static compressive capacity, and reduces static subsidence tendency under the reported conditions.
study.study_design: CT-derived healthy L1-L5 lumbar finite-element model from one 26-year-old male (85 kg, 180 cm), postoperative L3-resection models with either traditional or Gyroid AVI, 400 N plus 10 Nm flexion/extension/bending/torsion simulations, and selective-laser-melted Ti6Al4V specimens (three replicates per type) tested in ASTM-style static compression and polyurethane-foam subsidence tests.
study.sample_or_model: One healthy adult male CT anatomy for intact and postoperative FEM; Ti6Al4V Gyroid and traditional porous AVI specimens, target porosity 60%, three printed replicates per design; Grade 15 polyurethane foam block as a cancellous-bone surrogate for subsidence. No animal implantation, clinical cohort, fatigue test, or human outcome endpoint is included.
comparators: Traditional strut-based/diamond-like porous AVI versus TPMS Gyroid AVI with the same external contour
Intact L1-L5 spine versus postoperative L3-resection reconstruction
Upper and lower bone-prosthetic interfaces across flexion, extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation
CAD-designed 60% porosity versus measured specimen porosity (58.9 +/- 0.53% traditional; 59.4 +/- 0.41% Gyroid)
Static compression failure and 3 mm subsidence in polyurethane foam; no cyclic or in-vivo comparator
method_spine: Define Gyroid implicit-surface parameters, nominal 60% porosity, estimated pore size about 725 micrometres, and an external contour matched to the traditional AVI.
Build and mesh an L1-L5 healthy lumbar FEM with cortical/cancellous/endplate/cartilage/disc/ligament components and literature material properties.
Create postoperative L3/L3-L4-resection models with pedicle screws/rods and either porous AVI, using bonded bone-prosthetic contact to represent a healed phase.
Apply 400 N and 10 Nm loading for flexion, extension, bending, and torsion; validate only global ROM against published human/FE ranges.
Fabricate Ti6Al4V by SLM, heat treat/clean, measure porosity, and test static compression and 3 mm polyurethane-foam subsidence with n=3 specimens per architecture.

verification: The healthy lumbar model's ROM was compared with published human and FE values for flexion, extension, bending, and torsion (S009:C01); this verifies global kinematic plausibility, not local implant stress.
Measured porosity checks the printed specimens against nominal CAD design; Gyroid was 59.4 +/- 0.41% versus 60% target and traditional was 58.9 +/- 0.53% (S012:C01).
calibration: Material properties were taken from literature tables and the postoperative model used a 100 MPa bone-graft value; no specimen-specific calibration to interface stress or subsidence was reported (S004:C01; S005:C01).
The Gyroid bias constant and 60% target were selected from the design relation, not optimized against a clinical load history or measured pore-size distribution (S003:C01).
validation: ROM agreement is an external comparison for the intact model only; postoperative stress fields and implant failure predictions were not independently validated against vertebral specimens (S009:C01-S011:C01).

Static compression and polyurethane-foam subsidence provide matched experimental checks of the two printed architectures, but they do not validate fatigue, osseointegration, or clinical subsidence (S008:C01; S013:C01-S014:C01).
sensitivity: Loading-direction sensitivity is sampled across flexion, extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation, with 400 N and 10 Nm conditions (S006:C01; S010:C01-S011:C01).
No systematic sensitivity to anatomy, endplate quality, contact friction, mesh, material uncertainty, pore-size deviation, load magnitude, fatigue history, or implant height is reported.
application_prediction: Lower modeled stress and higher static loads are used to predict reduced mechanical-failure and subsidence risk after vertebral replacement; they are not clinical event measurements (S010:C01-S015:C02).
The conclusion's promising clinical-treatment language is an application prediction requiring in-vivo and long-term patient validation (S015:C02; S016:C01).

primary_outcomes: The Gyroid design used a 60% nominal porosity and an estimated pore size around 725 micrometres from the bias-constant relation; the packet does not report a direct as-built pore-size measurement (S003:C01).

Measured porosity was 58.9 +/- 0.53% for traditional porous AVI and 59.4 +/- 0.41% for Gyroid, both within about 3% of target; semi-molten powder contributed to the shortfall from CAD design (S012:C01).

At bone-prosthetic interfaces, Gyroid peak stress was lower except during left bending and left torsion; reported reductions at upper/lower interfaces ranged from 3.3% to 15.5% for selected directions (S010:C01).

Within the prosthesis, Gyroid peak stress reductions versus traditional porous AVI were 63.8% flexion, 46.8% extension, 73.4% left bending, 61.0% right bending, 42.1% left rotation, and 72.4% right rotation; traditional stress concentrated at porous-frame junctions whereas Gyroid stress was more uniform (S011:C01).

Static subsidence load at 3 mm in Grade 15 polyurethane foam was 2660 +/- 8 N for traditional and 3158 +/- 10 N for Gyroid, a 15.7% higher load for Gyroid and a surrogate reduction in subsidence tendency (S013:C01).

Static compression results were reported as 60.52 +/- 1.53 kN/mm for traditional and 98.4 +/- 2.3 kN/mm for Gyroid (38.51% higher; the abstract describes the ratio as about 1.63). The unit is reproduced as reported and is not clarified in the packet (S014:C01; S001:C01).

Traditional AVI fractured at the porous/frame junction by 1.5 mm compression displacement, whereas Gyroid failed at 3 mm mainly by a 45-degree shear fracture; these are monotonic static failure modes, not fatigue outcomes (S014:C01).
study.highest_evidence_level_reached: Verified global ROM plausibility plus comparative CT-based model predictions and n=3 static mechanical/surrogate-subsidence tests; no independent local-stress validation, cyclic durability, in-vivo osseointegration, clinical subsidence, or patient outcome is reached.

argument_map.central_claim: Under the specified healthy anatomy, bonded healed-phase contact, 400 N/10 Nm motions, SLM Ti6Al4V state, and monotonic tests, the Gyroid AVI distributes stress more uniformly and outperforms a strut-based porous AVI in static compression and polyurethane-foam subsidence resistance.
data: The two AVIs share external contour but differ in internal topology; nominal Gyroid porosity and pore size are design values, whereas measured porosity is reported separately (S003:C01; S012:C01).
FEM predicts lower implant and selected interface peak stresses across six loading directions, with exceptions at left bending/torsion for interfaces (S010:C01-S011:C01).
Three-specimen monotonic compression and foam subsidence tests report higher Gyroid loads and different failure locations (S007:C01-S008:C01; S013:C01-S014:C01).
argument_map.warrant: A topology comparison is persuasive for the tested architecture only when nominal versus as-built structure, model assumptions, loading, sample count, failure definition, and surrogate endpoint are kept explicit.
backing: The intact ROM comparison provides a limited global model check (S009:C01).
Traditional frame-junction fracture and Gyroid shear failure qualitatively align with the modeled stress concentration difference (S011:C01; S014:C01).
argument_map.qualifier: Comparative engineering evidence for one Gyroid/traditional pair under one anatomy and static test protocol; translational benefit remains predicted.
rebuttals_or_boundaries: The FEM uses one 26-year-old male anatomy, literature material properties, bonded bone-prosthetic contact, fixed L5, and simplified loading; inter-individual and postoperative variability are not represented (S004:C01-S006:C01).
ROM agreement does not validate local stress, subsidence, fusion, or failure timing.
Polyurethane foam is a cancellous-bone surrogate and 3 mm monotonic subsidence is an engineering proxy, not vertebral endplate subsidence in patients (S013:C01).
n=3 per printed design and a reported kN/mm compression unit ambiguity limit precision and comparability (S007:C01; S014:C01).

measured: As-built specimen porosity, monotonic load-displacement curves, 3 mm foam subsidence load, compression failure displacement, and failure mode are directly measured for three replicates per architecture (S007:C01-S008:C01; S012:C01; S013:C01-S014:C01).
ROM values are compared against published ranges for the intact model, while postoperative interface and implant stresses are model outputs rather than measurements (S009:C01-S011:C01).
predicted: FEM predicts vertebral-interface and implant von Mises stress under 400 N/10 Nm flexion, extension, bending, and torsion and uses a healed bonded interface assumption (S005:C01-S006:C01; S010:C01-S011:C01).

Lower stress, higher static load, and lower foam subsidence tendency are used to predict reduced clinical mechanical failure/subsidence risk; no clinical event is observed (S013:C01; S015:C01-S016:C01).
inferred: The continuously curved Gyroid surface is inferred to reduce junction stress concentration and improve load distribution relative to the strut architecture (S011:C01; S015:C01).
Higher foam load at 3 mm is inferred to indicate reduced vertebral subsidence tendency, although endplate fracture, bone remodeling, and patient loading are absent (S013:C01; S015:C01).

The Gyroid topology is inferred to meet daily-activity safety requirements from static strength and modeled stress below cited fatigue-strength ranges, but no cyclic implant fatigue test was performed (S015:C01).
recommended: Measure as-built pore size, strut/sheet thickness, surface powder, internal defects, heat-treated properties, and batch variability alongside nominal Gyroid equations.
Validate local stress and subsidence in cadaveric or animal vertebral models with endplate quality, friction/contact, cyclic physiological loading, fatigue, and fusion/osseointegration outcomes.
Test multiple Gyroid bias/porosity/height designs and anatomies, and report clear force versus stiffness units and uncertainty before clinical translation (S015:C02).
proxy_to_outcome_bridges: ROM agreement validates global kinematics only; it does not validate local bone-prosthetic stress or subsidence (S009:C01).
Peak von Mises stress is a model proxy for overload and failure risk, not fracture incidence, fatigue life, loosening, or fusion (S010:C01-S011:C01).
3 mm polyurethane-foam subsidence load is a surrogate for cancellous-bone support and does not substitute for vertebral endplate subsidence in vivo (S013:C01).
Monotonic compression capacity and failure displacement are static proxies, not cyclic durability or long-term mechanical failure rates (S014:C01).
overclaim_risks: 'Pore size around 725 micrometres' is a nominal/design estimate; measured porosity is reported, but as-built pore-size and internal defect distributions are not (S003:C01; S012:C01).

The 15.7% foam subsidence difference and 38.51% static compression difference can be overread as clinical subsidence or implant-survival reduction without vertebral/endplate validation (S013:C01-S014:C01).

Lower modeled stress in selected motions does not establish lower failure in patients, especially because left bending/torsion interface reductions were not favorable and contact was bonded (S010:C01; S005:C01).
A reported kN/mm compression-load unit and n=3 sample size limit confidence in the exact magnitude and generality of the static comparison (S014:C01).

section_moves.move: Separate nominal Gyroid geometry from as-built characterization
section_moves.execution: The design section defines a 60% nominal porosity and estimated 725 micrometre pore size, while fabrication/porosity sections measure printed mass-derived porosity and note semi-molten powder (S003:C01; S007:C01; S012:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: For lattice implants, keep CAD/implicit-surface targets, printed geometry, surface state, and measured properties on separate evidence rows.
section_moves.failure_mode: A nominal pore size or porosity can be mistaken for the structure actually tested or implanted.

section_moves.move: Validate the intact model before using postoperative stress predictions
section_moves.execution: The paper compares intact ROM with published human/FE data, then applies postoperative bonded-contact models and six loading conditions to compare the two AVIs (S004:C01-S006:C01; S009:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: Name exactly which model outputs are externally checked and do not transfer global kinematic agreement to local implant stress validation.
section_moves.failure_mode: A ROM match can be reported as validation of stress, fusion, or subsidence without a local measurement.

section_moves.move: Keep stress, static failure, and subsidence proxies separate
section_moves.execution: Interface/prosthesis stress reductions, foam 3 mm subsidence loads, and monotonic compression loads/failure modes are presented as distinct endpoints with different comparators and failure definitions (S010:C01-S014:C01).
section_moves.transferable_principle: Use an endpoint vector that prevents a static surrogate from standing in for clinical subsidence, fatigue, fixation, or fusion.
section_moves.failure_mode: A higher foam load or compression force can be compressed into a claim of lower clinical failure rate.

section_moves.move: Place topology advantages beside model and translation limits
section_moves.execution: The Discussion attributes smoother Gyroid stress distribution and higher static strength to continuous curvature but acknowledges one-anatomy FEM, one Gyroid design, and the need for in-vivo/long-term follow-up (S015:C01-S015:C02).
section_moves.transferable_principle: State the next discriminating model or experiment at the same endpoint level as each proposed clinical benefit.
section_moves.failure_mode: Calling a promising AVI a clinical treatment option before cyclic, endplate, fusion, and patient validation overstates evidence.

author_reported: The FEM is based on one individual's image data and may vary across the population.
Only one Gyroid design was investigated; other TPMS designs and optimal AVI features were not explored.
The study uses FEM and mechanical experiments without in-vivo or long-term patient validation, which the authors identify as necessary (S015:C02).
reader_identified: Only three printed replicates per architecture were tested; no power calculation, batch replication, or confidence intervals beyond mean +/- SD are reported.

The healthy model is one 26-year-old male with literature properties, fixed L5, 400 N/10 Nm loads, and bonded healed-phase contact; endplate damage, friction, fusion progression, and patient variability are absent.
Global ROM comparison does not independently validate postoperative local stress, contact mechanics, subsidence, or failure location.
The Gyroid pore size is estimated from the nominal equation and no direct as-built pore-size/strut-thickness distribution or internal-defect measurement is reported.
Static monotonic tests in Grade 15 polyurethane foam do not address cyclic fatigue, cadaveric endplates, bone remodeling, loosening, or fusion.
likely_bias_direction: Choosing one Gyroid design and a traditional strut comparator may favor the selected topology while leaving the broader TPMS design space unresolved.
Surrogate foam and bonded-contact assumptions likely make subsidence/fixation behavior more uniform than in osteoporotic or damaged human endplates.
Static n=3 mechanical tests may overstate reproducibility and underrepresent manufacturing defects or fatigue failures.
limitations.scope_boundary: The work supports a conditioned engineering comparison of one SLM Ti6Al4V Gyroid AVI against one traditional porous AVI in a single CT-based model and static surrogate tests. It does not establish clinical subsidence reduction, fusion, fatigue life, implant survival, or general superiority across patients and TPMS designs.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Keep nominal lattice equations, as-built porosity/surface state, and tested mechanical response in separate rows so a CAD target is not mistaken for an implanted structure.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Porous-design Methods, manufacturing Results, and reproducibility audit.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: A 725 micrometre pore estimate and 60% CAD porosity do not document direct as-built pore-size or defect distributions.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Build a mechanics endpoint vector that separates local FEM stress, global ROM verification, monotonic compression failure, and surrogate subsidence instead of treating them as one failure outcome.
writing_capability_candidates.manuscript_use: Computational validation, Results, and translational boundary writing.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: ROM agreement and a higher foam 3 mm load do not validate patient fusion, cyclic durability, or clinical subsidence reduction.

writing_capability_candidates.capability: Report topology comparisons with load-direction exceptions and failure-mode differences before summarizing a global advantage.
writing_capability_candidates.counterexample_or_boundary: Gyroid reduced most implant stress components but did not lower every interface direction and failed by a different shear mode at 3 mm.

critical_weaknesses: One CT anatomy and bonded healed-phase contact limit model generalizability.
n=3 static specimens per design and an ambiguous reported compression unit limit precision.
No direct as-built pore-size/defect characterization, cyclic fatigue, cadaveric/animal endplate model, fusion, or clinical follow-up.

summary_zh: 这是一项有限元与静态力学原始研究，不含动物或临床结局。两种外形相同的Ti-6Al-4V人工椎体分别采用传统杆状/diamond-like孔结构与名义60%孔隙、估计孔径约725 μm的Gyroid；实际质量法孔隙率为传统58.9±0.53%、Gyroid59.4±0.41%，未报告直接实测孔径。单一26岁男性CT模型在400 N+10 Nm各运动下显示Gyroid多数植体应力下降，但界面左侧弯曲/左旋转并非全面改善；n=3静态试验中3 mm聚氨酯泡沫沉降载荷3158±10 N对2660±8 N，压缩结果按原文单位kN/mm报告且存在单位歧义。沉降、静态断裂和有限元应力均是代理/预测，不等于临床融合、疲劳或失效率。
reader_notes: Primary Luna reader read every non-reference packet chunk in heading order: S001:C01 through S027:C01, including S015:C02 and all statements/ethics/data chunks.
Full text supports original computational plus static mechanical research; the metadata in-vivo/biological cues are not supported by an implantation experiment.
Nominal Gyroid structure, measured porosity, modeled stress, static compression failure, and polyurethane-foam subsidence are kept as distinct evidence states.
The reported compression-load unit kN/mm is preserved with an ambiguity note rather than silently converted; no references chunk was present.
